Introduction

Today's most capable open source language models all utilize a common architectural pattern: instead of one large "brain" with densely interconnected layers, they have many smaller specialized subnetworks per layer, and only activate a fraction of them for each token they process. This is called a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture [1][2]. The efficiency gain is substantial: the model has the capacity of its full size, but only runs a fraction of it on any given input. For quite some time, TNG has been heavily invested in researching how to make use of the modular structure of MoE models, see also our publications on Mixtures of Tunable Experts [3] and Assembly of Experts [4], as well as our Chimera models [5]. In particular, targeted control, selection or extension of experts seems within reach.
There's a catch, though. The "experts" in MoE models usually are not experts in the way a human would understand the term: they do not strictly specialize in a programming language, physics, legal text, or some other domain. They emerge during pretraining, and we have no direct control over what they learn. However, results by the Allen Institute for AI from earlier this year [6] demonstrate that domain-specific experts are indeed possible and practical. Hence we ask: What if we have a capable model that is great at most things, but weak in a specific domain, say, Rust or Haskell programming? Can we add a new expert, or a few of them, for just that domain, without touching the rest of the model?
We show that the answer to the questions just raised is yes. We extended Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base with new experts specifically trained for Rust and Haskell, achieving significant improvements on language-specific benchmarks with no drop in baseline capabilities. More importantly, these experts are modular building blocks: you can train them independently, drop them into the model, and combine multiple experts from different domains into a single checkpoint, all without retraining.
The longer-term vision is an ecosystem of composable experts: a frozen, capable base model, plus a growing library of drop-in domain experts that can be added, exchanged, or removed on demand. Adding a new capability no longer requires retraining the base model or modifying anything else.

Why Not Just Fine-Tune?

The standard approach to giving a model a new capability is fine-tuning, i.e., training some or all of its weights on domain-specific data. The most popular lightweight variant is Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [7]. Here, the base model is frozen and only small trainable adapters are injected that modify the base's weights.
This works well for a single domain. The problem is composition. When two LoRA adapters are trained independently for different domains, they modify the same shared weights. This causes interference when we combine them. Averaging two adapters can leave one domain behind; summing them can degrade the base model. Neither approach reliably recovers both domains at once.
Our approach is different. Instead of modifying shared weights, we add new weights alongside the existing ones, in a separate parameter space. The model's router, which is the mechanism that decides which subnetworks to activate for each token, learns when to call on the new expert and when to rely on the base model. Because the new expert lives in its own parameter space, there is nothing to reconcile when combining experts: composition is simply concatenation.

How It Works

We start with a pretrained MoE model and keep its base weights frozen. We then add one or more new experts alongside the existing ones, plus the small routing weights that tell the model when to use them. Only these new components are trained, which correspond to roughly 125 million parameters per expert on our 35 billion parameter test model.
The new experts compete for tokens with the base experts: the router scores all experts, both old and new, and selects the best ones for each token.
By training the new router rows, the router learns when the new expert should be active. If a token does not belong to the new domain, the router selects the old experts, and the base model behaves almost exactly as before.

   
   Figure 1: We add experts and corresponding router rows (blue) to each layer of an MoE model. Only these added parameters are trainable.

A key practical challenge is the cold-start problem: a brand-new expert is not useful yet, so the router would quickly learn to turn it off. This would halt training before it begins. We solve this by initializing the new expert and the new router row from the most active existing expert and its router row in each layer. This gives the weights a known useful starting point. We briefly freeze the router so the new expert has time to learn useful behavior on the new domain before the router can decide to switch it off.
After training, the new expert weights are simply concatenated onto the base model's expert tensors. The result is a standard Hugging Face checkpoint with a few more experts. This is just a configuration change and does not need custom inference code.

Training

We trained our experts on Rust and Haskell subsets of The Stack v1 (deduplicated), using NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel, a PyTorch-native training framework. We use a sequence length of 4096 tokens. We trained data-parallel on a B200 node with 8 GPUs. Training new experts for a single domain takes roughly half a day.

Results

We evaluated our experts on a domain-specific code generation task (reporting pass@1) and a seven-task general-capability suite (ARC Easy/Challenge, BoolQ, HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, WinoGrande) to check for regressions.

Domain Improvements

The Rust expert raises Rust code generation from 0.62 to 0.73 (pass@1), and the Haskell expert raises Haskell from 0.32 to 0.51. On the general-capability suite, both experts stay within noise of the base model. The new capabilities come at no cost to existing ones.

Combining Experts

This is where the approach shines. We combined our best Rust and Haskell experts, which were trained independently, into a single checkpoint. The combined model holds both domain gains: 0.70 on Rust and 0.50 on Haskell (pass@1), staying close to the individual expert models, while general capabilities remain at the baseline level.
Then, we did a brief retraining of the new router rows on the combined model using mixed data (50/50 Rust and Haskell). This was meant to help the model balance the two domains and did fully restore the Rust and baseline capabilities and could even surpass the Haskell capabilities. No retraining of the new experts was needed after adapting the new router rows.

   
   Figure 3: Two independently trained experts, combined into one checkpoint. Both domain gains are recovered, and general capabilities remain at the baseline.

Comparison with LoRA

For comparison, we fine-tuned LoRA adapters on the same base model and data, sweeping over learning rate and adapter rank. The best Rust LoRA adapter reaches 0.74 on Rust; the best Haskell LoRA reaches 0.48 on Haskell, similar to our extra domain experts. General capabilities are maintained fairly well, reaching 0.78 for Rust LoRA and 0.77 for Haskell LoRA.
The bigger difference is seen after composition. When we average the two LoRA adapters, the domain capabilities almost collapse back to the base model, reaching 0.67 in Rust and 0.36 in Haskell. General capabilities are maintained. Summing the two LoRA adapters is worse: here, the model fares significantly worse than the base model in Rust, and also scores less with respect to Haskell and general capabilities.
Neither LoRA merge maintains both domains simultaneously. The combined experts hold both domain gains and the baseline score.

   
   Figure 4: Neither averaging nor summing can maintain the capabilities of the individual LoRA adapters.

Future Work

Our results point to two directions for follow-up work.
First, we have so far only added experts during continued pretraining. It remains to be seen whether they retain their performance after a full post-training pipeline, without losing their specialization or interfering with each other.
Second, we have focused on two programming languages, but the same approach should in principle extend to other languages and to non-code domains. Scaling to a larger number of coexisting experts, and checking whether they remain modular or start to interfere, is therefore a natural next step.

Conclusion

We have presented a method for extending pretrained MoE language models with domain-specific experts. The base model is frozen; new experts are grafted alongside it and trained independently per domain. The experts are modular building blocks: they can be trained separately, combined without retraining, and the result is a standard Hugging Face checkpoint that runs anywhere the base model runs.
On Rust and Haskell code generation, the experts deliver large gains over the base model while preserving general capabilities. While LoRA adapters fail to compose, our experts compose by construction because they live in a disjoint parameter space and combination is simply concatenation.
Various open questions remain, of course. For example, a simple appending of experts may harm inference efficiency by breaking expert parallelism, i.e., the efficient distribution of experts among GPUs, and expert load-balancing. However, combining it with simple pruning techniques (such as REAP [8]) may help here, so that instead of a simple expert extension an actual replacement of dispensable experts is done. And, of course, the actual goal is a modular MoE that can be extended cheaply with desired capabilities via composable experts. These are trained independently and combined on demand. Adding a new domain no longer requires touching the base model or retraining anything else.
